title: 4. Detecting abrupt change with actR
text:
actR (Abrupt Change Toolkit in R) can ask two kinds of questions of paleoclimate records:
actR will propagate uncertainty in the ages and the values with ensembles, and test results against null hypotheses: many surrogate series with the same spectral properties as the real record but no events. A result is significant if the real record shows the change more often than the surrogates do.
We’ll stay in western North America (AR6 region WNA) and:

title: 4. Detecting abrupt change with actR
text:
Setup

library(actR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

source(here::here("R/helpers.R"))
checkVersions()

options(cli.progress_show_after = Inf)  # hide progress bars in the rendered page

h2k <- h2kTimeseries()

title: 4. Detecting abrupt change with actR
text:
Shifts in a single record
Crevice Lake (Yellowstone) d18O covers the last 9,000 years. Larger d18O values mean less streamflow, so a step up means a shift to drier conditions.

crevice <- h2k |>
  filter(dataSetName == "LS08STCR", paleoData_variableName == "d18O")

lipdViz::mapTs(crevice, size = 4, lat.range = c(35, 55), lon.range = c(-125, -95))








detectShift() looks for changes in the mean with a changepoint algorithm (method = "PELT", from the changepoint package), on every member of an ensemble:

simulate.time.uncertainty and simulate.paleo.uncertainty build the ensemble by perturbing the ages and the values (paleo.uncertainty, in permil here).
minimum.segment.length is the shortest stretch of time, in years, that counts as a segment. This sets the timescale of the shifts you can find.
null.hypothesis.n is the number of surrogate series used to judge significance.

actR reads each record’s time and its metadata (see tutorial 1). time.units puts the axis on a chosen scale, here years CE, so that the results are in years CE whatever the record’s own units.

set.seed(4)
shifts <- detectShift(crevice,
                      time.units = "CE",
                      vals.variable.name = "d18O",
                      method = "PELT",
                      minimum.segment.length = 500,
                      simulate.time.uncertainty = TRUE,
                      simulate.paleo.uncertainty = TRUE,
                      paleo.uncertainty = 0.3,
                      n.ens = 50,
                      null.hypothesis.n = 50)

Keep n.ens and null.hypothesis.n small while you explore (50 here), and use several hundred for results you’ll report.
summary() lists the shifts that are significant at the 0.05 level:

summary(shifts)

LS08STCR - d18O: Shift in Mean results
Searched for Shift in Mean with a minimum segment length of 500 years, summarizing the results over windows of 100 years (yr AD).

Overall result: Detected 3 Shift in Mean event(s) that were significant at the alpha < 0.05 level
# A tibble: 3 × 4
  time_start time_end pvalue deltas
       <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1       -852     -752 0       1.03 
2      -4352    -4252 0.0200  0.995
3        148      248 0.0400  1.60 
Time uncertainty considered? TRUE Time ensemble generated in `propagateUncertainties()`)
Paleo uncertainty considered? TRUE Values ensemble generated in `propagateUncertainties()`)
Error propagation ensemble members = 50
Null hypothesis testing ensemble members = 50 
Members simulated using isospectral method

Parameter choices:
cpt.fun = changepoint::cpt.mean
minimum.segment.length = 500
method = PELT
penalty = MBIC
ncpts.max = Inf


plot() shows the record and its ensemble (top) and, in each time bin, the fraction of ensemble members with a shift there (bottom). Bars beyond the orange lines (the 90th and 95th percentiles of the surrogates) are significant, and are drawn darker.

shift_plot <- plot(shifts)  # plot() draws the figure; assigning it avoids drawing it twice








All three significant shifts are positive (the deltas column, younger minus older segment means): steps up in d18O, toward drier conditions. They are part of a long-term drying trend at Crevice Lake through the Holocene.






TipUsing a real age ensemble



Here actR simulated age uncertainty. If you built an age ensemble in tutorial 3, put it in an ageEnsemble (yr BP) or yearEnsemble column of the tibble, and actR will use it instead.

title: 4. Detecting abrupt change with actR
text:
An excursion in one record
The tutorial 2 composite has a pronounced dry spell in the mid-1100s. Did a given record depart from its baseline then?
detectExcursion() compares an event window with reference windows on either side. An excursion is n.consecutive points in the event window beyond sig.num standard deviations from the reference mean.
First, prepare the records. As in tutorial 2, choose the WNA moisture records with lipdR::filterByInterpretation(), and use compositeR::interpDirectionSign() to flip each one so that larger values mean wetter. That way a negative excursion always means drier.

recs <- h2k |>
  filter(ar6_region == "WNA") |>
  lipdR::filterByInterpretation(isMoisture(variable), scope = "climate", match = "primary") |>
  mutate(direction = purrr::map_dbl(seq_len(n()), \(i) compositeR::interpDirectionSign(pick(everything())[i, ]))) |>
  filter(!is.na(direction)) |>
  distinct(dataSetName, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  clipTime(850, 1450) |>
  mutate(paleoData_values = purrr::map2(paleoData_values, direction, `*`))

Tree rings are annual and lake records are often decadal or coarser. In annual data, year-to-year variability is large compared with a multi-decade drought, and an excursion test on the raw series mostly measures that noise. So we average every record into 10-year bins with ens::bin(), which also puts trees and lakes on a comparable footing. time now holds the bin centers, so we set timeVariableName to "time", telling lipdR that time is its own source and not a copy of year or age (see tutorial 1):

binvec <- seq(850, 1450, by = 10)

decadal <- function(time, vals) {
  b <- ens::bin(time, vals, bin.vec = binvec)
  b[is.finite(b[, 2]), , drop = FALSE]
}

binned <- purrr::map2(recs$time, recs$paleoData_values, decadal)
recs <- recs |>
  mutate(time = purrr::map(binned, \(b) b[, 1]),
         paleoData_values = purrr::map(binned, \(b) b[, 2]),
         timeVariableName = "time") |>
  filter(purrr::map_int(paleoData_values, length) >= 30)   # at least 300 years of decades

nrow(recs)

[1] 19


Now test one record, the Beef Basin tree-ring streamflow reconstruction (Meko et al., 2007). The event window is 1120 to 1180 CE (event.yr = 1150, event.window = 60), and the reference windows are the 150 years on each side.

beef <- filter(recs, dataSetName == "BeefBasin.Meko.2007")

set.seed(4)
exc <- detectExcursion(beef,
                       time.units = "CE",
                       event.yr = 1150,
                       event.window = 60,
                       ref.window = 150,
                       exc.type = "negative",
                       sig.num = 1.5,
                       n.consecutive = 2,
                       min.vals = 5,
                       simulate.time.uncertainty = FALSE,
                       simulate.paleo.uncertainty = TRUE,
                       paleo.uncertainty = 0.2,
                       n.ens = 50,
                       null.hypothesis.n = 50)


summary(exc)

BeefBasin.Meko.2007 - tree-ring index: Excursion test results
Searched for negative excursions in a 60 years window around 1150 yr AD, with reference windows of 150 years on either side.

Overall result: Empirical p-value = 0
Time uncertainty considered? FALSE
Paleo uncertainty considered? TRUE
Parametric uncertainty considered? FALSE
Error propagation ensemble members = 50
Null hypothesis testing ensemble members = 50

Parameter choices:
sig.num = 1.5
n.consecutive = 2
exc.type = negative
min.vals = 5
na.rm = TRUE



plot(exc)








The red lines are the reference means and the thresholds (sig.num standard deviations). Points beyond the threshold in the event window count toward an excursion. event_probability is the fraction of ensemble members with an excursion, and the p-value compares it with the surrogates.
We don’t simulate age uncertainty here, since tree rings are precisely dated. For a lake or speleothem record, set simulate.time.uncertainty = TRUE or supply an age ensemble.






NoteChoosing the windows



min.vals is the fewest points needed in each window. With decadal bins, a 60-year event window holds 6 points; a 40-year window holds only 4 and wouldn’t be tested at min.vals = 5. sig.num, n.consecutive and the windows can also be given as vectors, one value per ensemble member (e.g. sig.num = rnorm(50, 1.5, 0.1)), so that the choice of parameters becomes part of the uncertainty.

title: 4. Detecting abrupt change with actR
section: The same test across the region
text:
The same test across the region
Run the same test on every record. split() turns the tibble into a list of one-row tibbles, and purrr::map() runs detectExcursion() on each. Records with too few points in the windows return no p-value.

set.seed(4)
events <- recs |>
  split(seq_len(nrow(recs))) |>
  purrr::map(\(r) detectExcursion(r,
                                  time.units = "CE",
                                  event.yr = 1150,
                                  event.window = 60,
                                  ref.window = 150,
                                  exc.type = "negative",
                                  sig.num = 1.5,
                                  n.consecutive = 2,
                                  min.vals = 5,
                                  simulate.time.uncertainty = FALSE,
                                  simulate.paleo.uncertainty = TRUE,
                                  paleo.uncertainty = 0.2,
                                  n.ens = 50,
                                  null.hypothesis.n = 50)) |>
  purrr::list_rbind() |>
  filter(!is.na(pvalue))


events |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  select(dataSetName, archiveType, event_probability, pvalue) |>
  arrange(pvalue)


  



Individually, only a few records are significant. Many records weakly pointing the same way can still add up to strong evidence, and that’s what the next step tests.

title: 4. Detecting abrupt change with actR
text:
A regional significance map
spatialSigTest() combines the records near each point on a grid. It weights each record by its distance (zero beyond distance.cutoff), adds up their event probabilities, and compares the sum with the same sum for the surrogates (agg.method = "robustNull"). distanceGrid() sets up the grid and the distances.

lon.range <- c(-126, -100)
lat.range <- c(30, 50)

grid <- distanceGrid(events, lon.range = lon.range, lat.range = lat.range, grid.resolution = 1)

pval_grid <- purrr::map(grid,
                        spatialSigTest,
                        events = events,
                        agg.method = "robustNull",
                        use.weights = TRUE,
                        distance.cutoff = 500)

plotSignificance() maps the result. It returns a list, and the map is in $plot. Grid cells show the regional p-value for a negative (dry) excursion, more transparent where fewer records are nearby; points show each record’s own p-value.

sig <- plotSignificance(pval_grid,
                        sigTestResults = events,
                        which.test = "pvalNeg",
                        color.breaks = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2),
                        restrict.sites = TRUE,
                        alpha.by.weight = TRUE,
                        cutoff.distance = 500,
                        x.lim = lon.range,
                        y.lim = lat.range)

sig$plot +
  ggtitle("Dry excursion, 1120 to 1180 CE") +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA))








The mid-1100s drought is significant across the Colorado Plateau and the Four Corners, where several tree-ring records agree, but not in the north or along the coast.

title: 4. Detecting abrupt change with actR
text:
Try this

Test the late-1500s megadrought: event.yr = 1585, with clipTime() and binvec adjusted to cover 1400 to 1800.
Use exc.type = "positive" to look for wet excursions, or "either".
Change distance.cutoff in spatialSigTest(). How sensitive is the map?
Give sig.num and n.consecutive as vectors (one value per ensemble member) so that the parameter choices become part of the uncertainty.
Run detectShift() on the tutorial 2 composite median, or on another long record such as Leviathan Cave (Leviathan.Lachniet.2014).

title: 2. Regional composites with compositeR
text:
A composite averages many records into one regional series. Done carefully, it keeps the shared signal, reduces the noise of individual records, and carries the uncertainties of the inputs through to the result. compositeR does this with ensembles: it repeats the whole bin, standardize and average procedure many times, each time drawing different age models and proxy values, so the spread of the results shows the uncertainty.
Here we build a composite of moisture-sensitive records from the IPCC AR6 region WNA (western North America), for the Common Era. The region is set in one place, so you can rerun everything for another region.

title: 2. Regional composites with compositeR
text:
Setup

library(lipdR)
library(compositeR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

source(here::here("R/helpers.R"))
checkVersions()

region <- "WNA"

h2kTimeseries() does the steps from tutorial 1 in one call: read the compilation, keep the 0.9.0 members, add AR6 regions, and put every record’s time in years CE.

h2k <- h2kTimeseries()
nrow(h2k)

[1] 716

title: 2. Regional composites with compositeR
text:
Choose the records
A composite only makes sense if the records measure the same thing, and if they all point the same way. Hydroclimate2k records are interpreted as many different variables (precipitation, streamflow, P/E, PDSI, lake level, …), and a large value means “wetter” for some and “drier” for others. For example, lake-water d18O usually rises when evaporation exceeds precipitation.
The interpretations handle this (see tutorial 1): variable says what a record measures, and direction says whether larger values mean more or less of it.
First, choose the records that measure moisture. The interpretation vocabulary isn’t standardized yet, so isMoisture() (in R/helpers.R) recognizes the variants. It is TRUE for variables like precipitation, streamflow, P/E, PDSI and lake level, and FALSE for temperature, the isotopic composition of precipitation, and missing interpretations:

isMoisture(c("streamflow", "P/E", "Precipitation amount", "temperature", "precipitationIsotope", NA))

[1]  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE


lipdR::filterByInterpretation() applies it to each record’s interpretations. We want the records whose main climate interpretation is moisture, so we look only at climate-scoped interpretations (scope = "climate"), and only at the top one of those (match = "primary"). With the default, match = "any", a record whose second climate interpretation mentions moisture would be included too.
Then the direction. compositeR::interpDirectionSign() reads a record’s interpretation direction and returns +1 if larger values mean more of the variable, -1 if they mean less, and NA if the direction is missing or ambiguous. It accepts “positive”/“negative” and “increase”/“decrease” in any capitalization.
Ideally, all the directions would be “positive” or “negative”, a curation to-do.
Select the region’s moisture records, one per dataset, and keep the Common Era:

recs <- h2k |> #Start with the full tibble
  filter(ar6_region == region) |> #filter to this region
  filterByInterpretation(isMoisture(variable), scope = "climate", match = "primary") |> #keep records interpreted as moisture
  mutate(direction = purrr::map_dbl(seq_len(n()), \(i) compositeR::interpDirectionSign(pick(everything())[i, ]))) |> #+1 or -1
  filter(!is.na(direction)) |> #drop records without a usable direction
  distinct(dataSetName, .keep_all = TRUE) |> #drop duplicates
  clipTime(0, 2000) |>
  filter(purrr::map_int(time, length) > 20) #only look at those with more than 20 datapoints in the interval

recs |>
  select(dataSetName, archiveType, paleoData_variableName,
         interpretation1_variable, interpretation1_direction, direction)


  



The table shows the interpretation1_ columns, but the scope matters. interpDirectionSign() also uses the climate-scoped interpretation by default. Abbott.Hiner.2016 shows why: its first interpretation is environmental (winter wetness and/or runoff intensity, with no direction), and its second is climatic (winter precipitation, positive), so it gets +1. getInterpretations() shows all of a record’s interpretations:

getInterpretations(filter(recs, dataSetName == "Abbott.Hiner.2016")) |>
  select(dataSetName, number, scope, variable, direction)


  









ImportantLook at what you’re compositing



isMoisture() is a convenience for handling our currently imperfect metadata. It’s not ideal. Read the table above, and check the interpretations of any record you aren’t sure about. Watch out for drought indices: “drought, positive” means larger values are drier, so isMoisture() leaves them out rather than let them point the wrong way.



lipdViz::mapTs(recs, color = "archiveType", size = 4,
               lat.range = c(25, 55), lon.range = c(-130, -100))

title: 2. Regional composites with compositeR
text:
Records in different units
The records are in different units (mm of streamflow, permil, tree-ring indices), some were dated in yr BP and some in years CE, and half of them point the “wrong” way. We don’t need to fix any of this before compositing:

Units: the standardization step (below) puts every record in standard-deviation units, and we give the uncertainty in standard deviations too (uncUnits = "sd").
Time: compositeEnsembles() reads each record’s time and its scale, and puts it on the scale given by time.units. Here that’s "CE", so binvec is in years CE. (Without time.units, it uses the scale the records share, or yr BP if they differ.)
Direction: compositeEnsembles() flips records with a negative direction when alignInterpDirection = TRUE (the default), using interpDirectionSign().

It also takes the tibble directly. You can pass a lipdR timeseries list from extractTs() instead.

title: 2. Regional composites with compositeR
text:
Build the composite
compositeEnsembles() repeats these steps nens times:

Bin each record onto a common time axis (binvec). The default binFun, sampleEnsembleThenBinTs(), first perturbs each record: it adds autocorrelated noise to the values (uncVar = 0.5 with uncUnits = "sd": half of each record’s standard deviation, whatever its units), and it simulates age uncertainty with the Banded Age Model (BAM), except for tree rings and documents, whose ages are exact. Records with a negative interpretation direction are flipped at this step.
Standardize the binned records with stanFun. Here standardizeOverInterval() gives every record mean 0 and standard deviation 1 over 1600 to 1950 CE, a period all the records cover.
Average the standardized records in each bin.


binvec <- seq(0, 2000, by = 20)

set.seed(2026)
comp <- compositeEnsembles(recs,
                           binvec = binvec,
                           nens = 50,
                           time.units = "CE",
                           uncVar = 0.5,
                           uncUnits = "sd",
                           stanFun = standardizeOverInterval,
                           interval = c(1600, 1950),
                           verbose = FALSE)

nens = 50 keeps this quick. Use several hundred for real work.
The standard deviation behind uncUnits = "sd" is the SD of each whole record, over the years we kept. A record with a large trend has a large SD, so it gets more noise. If you know a record’s measurement or calibration uncertainty, put it in a column and name that column in uncVar instead (in the record’s own units).






NoteAbout the age uncertainty



BAM was designed for layer-counted records, such as corals and varves. For radiometrically dated lake and speleothem records it gives only a rough idea of age uncertainty. If a record has an age ensemble (see tutorial 3), put it in an ageEnsemble column (yr BP, as a matrix), and compositeEnsembles() will draw from it instead.
Tree rings and historical documents are precisely dated, so their ages are used as they are. The exactAgeArchives argument of sampleEnsembleThenBinTs() controls which archive types this applies to.

title: 2. Regional composites with compositeR
text:
Plot it
plotComposite() draws the composite’s ensemble as quantile ribbons, plus how many records contribute to each bin. The composite knows its time scale (comp$timeUnits), so plotComposite(comp) gives a forward year CE axis. Here we take the two panels separately (combine = FALSE), so that we can give them matching axes and labels:

panels <- plotComposite(comp, combine = FALSE)

ce_axis <- scale_x_continuous("Year (CE)", limits = c(0, 2000), expand = c(0, 0))

egg::ggarrange(
  panels$compositeEns + ce_axis + labs(x = NULL, y = "Moisture anomaly (SD)") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50"),
  panels$dataUsed + ce_axis,
  ncol = 1, heights = c(2, 1),
  top = paste(region, "moisture composite")
)








summary() gives the composite’s quantiles in each bin:

comp_summary <- summary(comp)
head(comp_summary)


  



Notice the droughts in the 1100s and in the late 1200s, and the wetter conditions before about 1100 CE. Western North America’s medieval megadroughts are well known from tree rings, and here lake records support them too. The uncertainty widens before 800 CE, where fewer records contribute.

title: 2. Regional composites with compositeR
text:
Does every archive agree?
A useful check is to composite each archive on its own. If trees and lakes tell different stories, that is worth understanding before you trust the combined result.

by_archive <- purrr::map(c("Wood", "LakeSediment"), function(a) {
  sub <- filter(recs, archiveType == a)
  set.seed(2026)
  ca <- compositeEnsembles(sub,
                           binvec = binvec,
                           nens = 50,
                           time.units = "CE",
                           uncVar = 0.5,
                           uncUnits = "sd",
                           stanFun = standardizeOverInterval,
                           interval = c(1600, 1950),
                           verbose = FALSE)
  s <- summary(ca)
  s$archive <- paste0(a, " (n = ", nrow(sub), ")")
  s
}) |>
  bind_rows()

binning and aligning the data. This may take some time depending on the number of records (n = 17) and number of ensembles (n = 50)
binning and aligning the data. This may take some time depending on the number of records (n = 8) and number of ensembles (n = 50)

names(by_archive)[2:4] <- c("lo", "med", "hi")

ggplot(by_archive, aes(x = age, fill = archive, color = archive)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.25, color = NA) +
  geom_line(aes(y = med)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey50") +
  scale_x_continuous("Year (CE)", limits = c(0, 2000), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(y = "Moisture anomaly (SD)", fill = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

title: 2. Regional composites with compositeR
text:
Try this

Change region at the top to another AR6 region (NWN, ENA, MED, EAS, …) and rerun everything. Check the record table first.
Use stanFun = standardizeOverRandomInterval with duration = 300, searchRange = c(1000, 1950), which picks a different standardization window for each ensemble member, so that the choice of window becomes part of the uncertainty.
Try samplePct = 0.75, which leaves out a random quarter of the records in each ensemble member (a jackknife).
Weight records with weights = "archiveType", so that each archive type counts equally however many records it has.

title: Before the workshop
text: Do this at home or in the office, on a good connection. It takes 10 to 20 minutes, mostly package installation.

title: Before the workshop
text:
1. Get the tutorials
Either clone the repository:
git clone https://github.com/nickmckay/hydroclimate2k-analysis-tutorials.git
or download it as a zip and unzip it.
Open hydroclimate2k-analysis-tutorials.Rproj in RStudio (or open the folder in Positron). Working inside the project matters: the helper functions use it to find the data/ folder.

title: Before the workshop
text:
2. Run the preflight script
In R, from the project folder:
source("R/preflight.R")
or in a terminal:
Rscript R/preflight.R
The script:

installs or updates lipdR, ens, lipdViz, agemodelR, geoChronR, compositeR and actR from GitHub, plus a few CRAN packages (sf, dplyr, ggplot2 and friends);
checks that the versions are new enough;
downloads the Hydroclimate2k compilation (version 0.9.0, about 280 MB) and its BibTeX citations into data/, unzips and reads it, and saves a fast-loading .rds copy;
downloads the IPCC AR6 reference regions.

When it finishes it prints the package versions. You should see lipdR 0.8.4 or newer and geoChronR 2.0.0 or newer.






TipInstalling from GitHub



If install_github() complains about the GitHub API rate limit, create a personal access token with usethis::create_github_token() and store it with gitcreds::gitcreds_set(), then run the script again.
On Windows you need Rtools for packages that compile code.

title: Before the workshop
text:
If the data download fails
The compilation lives at
https://lipdverse.org/export/downloads/hydroclimate2k/0_9_0/hydroclimate2k0_9_0.zip
If R cannot download it (this happened on some Windows machines in early November 2026, because of a certificate-revocation server outage), download it in your web browser and move it to the data/ folder of the project, keeping the name hydroclimate2k0_9_0.zip. Then run the preflight script again. It will skip the download and read the file you saved.
You can also read it without the helpers, from wherever you saved it. readLipd() doesn’t open local zip files, so unzip it first:
unzip("~/Downloads/hydroclimate2k0_9_0.zip", exdir = "~/Downloads/hydroclimate2k0_9_0")
D <- lipdR::readLipd("~/Downloads/hydroclimate2k0_9_0")

title: Hydroclimate2k analysis tutorials
text:
These tutorials show how to analyze the Hydroclimate2k compilation in R, using the LiPD family of packages. They were written for the Hydroclimate2k workshop at UBC, Vancouver (November 9 to 11, 2026), but work for anyone.
Each tutorial runs from a fresh R session and reads the compilation from a local copy, so once you have run the setup step you can work offline.

title: Hydroclimate2k analysis tutorials
text:
Start here

Follow Before the workshop: install the packages and download the data (about 280 MB). Please do this before you arrive, because conference wifi will not cope with a room full of people downloading at once.
Work through the tutorials in order. Tutorial 1 introduces the data and the helper functions the others use.

title: Hydroclimate2k analysis tutorials
text:
The packages
The LiPD family was reorganized and synchronized in November 2026. geoChronR is now a thin wrapper that loads four smaller packages:



Package
What it does




lipdR
Read, write, extract and filter LiPD data


ens
Ensembles, binning, time-axis conversion, age-uncertain correlation and regression


lipdViz
Maps and plots


agemodelR
Age models (Bacon, Bchron, BAM)


geoChronR
Loads all four of the above


compositeR
Compositing records into regional or global means


actR
Shift and excursion detection









WarningOld scripts may break



You need lipdR 0.8.4 or newer and geoChronR 2.0.0 or newer. lipdR 0.7 renamed the compilation fields (inCompilationBeta became inCompilation), added filterByCompilation(), and removed 27 functions. The old geoChronR (1.1.x) installs under the same name, so check packageVersion("geoChronR").
lipdR 0.8 records the time scale (yr BP, ka, year CE, …) of every time column, and gives every timeseries a standard time column. lipdViz, compositeR and actR use it by default, and take time.units to choose the scale, so records dated in yr BP and in year CE can be plotted and analyzed together. Tutorial 1 explains how it works.
lipdR 0.8.4 adds filterByInterpretation(), which selects records by their interpretations (for example, the records whose primary climate interpretation is precipitation), whichever number the interpretation has in each record. See tutorial 1.

title: Hydroclimate2k analysis tutorials
text:
Getting help
Open an issue on this repository, or find Nick at the workshop.

title: 1. Loading, exploring, plotting and mapping
text: This tutorial reads the Hydroclimate2k compilation into R, narrows it down to the records in the compilation, finds which IPCC AR6 region each record is in, and makes maps and timeseries plots. The later tutorials build on these steps.

title: 1. Loading, exploring, plotting and mapping
text:
Packages and helpers

library(lipdR)    # read, extract and filter LiPD data
library(lipdViz)  # maps and plots
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

source(here::here("R/helpers.R"))
checkVersions()

R/helpers.R holds a few small functions shared by all the tutorials. checkVersions() stops with a message if any of the LiPD packages is too old.

title: 1. Loading, exploring, plotting and mapping
text:
Read the compilation
The compilation is distributed as a zip file of LiPD files (one per dataset) on lipdverse.org. You can read it straight from the web:

options(timeout = 1800)  # it's about 280 MB, so allow more than R's default 60 s
D <- readLipd("https://lipdverse.org/export/downloads/hydroclimate2k/0_9_0/hydroclimate2k0_9_0.zip")

or from a copy you have downloaded. readLipd() can’t open a local zip file, so unzip it first and read the folder of .lpd files:

unzip("data/hydroclimate2k0_9_0.zip", exdir = "data/hydroclimate2k0_9_0")
D <- readLipd("data/hydroclimate2k0_9_0")

In these tutorials we use getHydroclimate2k(), which does all of this once (download, unzip, read) and keeps a fast-loading copy in data/:

D <- getHydroclimate2k()
length(D)

[1] 484


D is a multi-LiPD object: a named list with one element per dataset. Each dataset holds its metadata (geo, pub, archiveType, …) and its data tables (paleoData, chronData).

names(D)[1:5]

[1] "AB08MEN01"              "Abbott.Hiner.2016"      "Akcakalecave.Jex.2011" 
[4] "AlbercaLake.Wogau.2019" "Altiplano.Morales.2012"

L <- D[[1]]
L$dataSetName

[1] "AB08MEN01"

L$archiveType

[1] "Coral"

L$geo$latitude

[1] -0.13

L$geo$longitude

[1] 98.52

title: 1. Loading, exploring, plotting and mapping
text:
From datasets to timeseries
Most analyses work on timeseries: one variable (a column of a data table) together with its time axis and all the metadata above it. extractTs() pulls every column out of every dataset, and ts2tibble() turns the result into a data frame, one row per timeseries.

TS <- extractTs(D)
length(TS)

[1] 3947

ts_all <- ts2tibble(TS)
dim(ts_all)

[1] 3947  722


Most of those columns are not climate records: they are depths, ages, sample IDs, and variables that the curators did not choose for the compilation. Membership is recorded in each timeseries’ inCompilation fields, which list the compilations it belongs to and, for each, the versions it has been part of. filterByCompilation() keeps the members.

filterByCompilation(ts_all, "hydroclimate2k") |> nrow()

[1] 717


That includes a timeseries that was in earlier versions but left the compilation. To get exactly the members of the version we downloaded, give the version too. Versions are written with underscores, as in the file names (h2k_version is "0_9_0"):

h2k <- filterByCompilation(ts_all, "hydroclimate2k",
                           version = h2k_version, version.op = "==") |>
  tibble::as_tibble()
nrow(h2k)

[1] 716








WarningUse underscores in the version



version = "0.9.0" (with dots) currently matches nothing and returns an empty table without an error. Use "0_9_0".


The tibble::as_tibble() at the end turns lipdR’s timeseries tibble into a plain tibble, which prints more compactly and works with all of dplyr.

1. Loading, exploring, plotting and mapping
text:
Maps
mapTs() maps a set of timeseries, colored by any column. Here we color by archive type.

mapTs(h2k, color = "archiveType", size = 3)








mapLipd() maps datasets instead of timeseries:

mapLipd(D, size = 3, label.site = FALSE)








Both return ggplot2 objects, so you can add to them. Here are the AR6 region outlines, which tell you where each region’s boundaries fall:

mapTs(h2k, color = "archiveType", size = 3) +
  geom_sf(data = regions, inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = NA, color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.2)

title: 1. Loading, exploring, plotting and mapping
text:
Time axes
Hydroclimate2k mixes records dated in years CE (tree rings, corals, documents, varves) with records dated in years before present (most lake and speleothem records; BP means before 1950). lipdR records the time scale of every time column when it reads a file, with four fields:

timeUnits: e.g. “yr AD”, “yr BP” or “ka”
timeDatum: the year CE of time zero (0 for CE, 1950 for BP)
timeDirection: “prograde” if time counts forward (year CE), “retrograde” if it counts back (yr BP)
timeExponent: 0 for years, 3 for ka (thousands of years)

extractTs() also gives every timeseries a time column: a copy of its primary time column, which timeVariableName names (usually age or year). timeSource says how its scale is known: from the file’s metadata, from its units, or “assumed” when the units don’t say.

h2k |>
  count(timeVariableName, timeUnits, timeDatum, timeDirection, timeExponent, timeSource)


  



Those few “assumed” records have time units that lipdR doesn’t recognize (for example “count/yr”), so it guessed year CE from the column name. That guess is right for all of them, but when it happens, lipdR warns once, and it’s worth checking.
With this information, lipdR converts between any two scales. convertTime() converts numbers:

convertTime(c(0, 50, 1000, 1950), from = "yr BP", to = "CE")

[1] 1950 1900  950    0

convertTime(c(1.2, 4.2), from = "ka", to = "CE")

[1]   750 -2250


and convertTsTime() converts the time of every record, and updates the metadata:

h2k_ce <- convertTsTime(h2k, "CE")
h2k_ce |>
  count(timeUnits)


  



The original age and year columns stay as they were. lipdViz, compositeR and actR all read time and its scale, so you usually don’t need to convert anything yourself: you tell each function which scale you want with time.units. They also take time.variable, to use another time column, such as age when time is year. h2kTimeseries() in R/helpers.R, which the later tutorials use, returns every record with time in years CE.






NoteIf you change time



Because time is a copy of its source column, lipdR checks that they still agree. If you edit time but not the source column, getTsTime() (and so every package) warns and uses the source column instead. So if you trim or rebin records, change both (clipTime() in R/helpers.R clips every column), or set timeVariableName to "time", which makes time its own source. Tutorial 4 does that after binning.

title: 1. Loading, exploring, plotting and mapping
text:
Overview plots
plotTimeAvailabilityTs() shows how many records cover each time, grouped by archive. It puts every record on the scale given by time.units, here years CE:

plotTimeAvailabilityTs(h2k, time.units = "CE", age.range = c(0, 2020), step = 10)








plotSummaryTs() combines the map and the availability plot:

summary_plot <- plotSummaryTs(h2k, time.units = "CE", age.range = c(0, 2020), step = 10, size = 3)








plotSummaryTs() draws the figure as it runs. We assign the result so R doesn’t also print a description of it.

title: 1. Loading, exploring, plotting and mapping
text:
Plot one record
plotTs() plots a single timeseries, on its own time scale by default. Here is a lake record dated in yr BP, plotted in years CE with yr BP as a second axis:

rec <- h2k |>
  filter(dataSetName == "Abbott.Hiner.2016", paleoData_variableName == "%sand")

plotTs(rec, time.units = "CE", secondary.axis = TRUE)








It returns a ggplot2 object, so you can change the labels or theme as usual.

text:
Try this

Map only one archive type, or color the map by interpretation1_variable.
Use filterByInterpretation() to find the records interpreted as temperature, and map them. How many have temperature as their primary interpretation (match = "primary")?
Pick another AR6 region and make its stack plot.
Use filterByCompilation() with a version to compare membership between versions.
D[["<dataSetName>"]] gets one dataset by name. Try getTables() on its paleoData to see all its measurement tables.

title: 3. Age uncertainty with geoChronR
text:
Most Hydroclimate2k records from lakes, speleothems and marine sediments are dated by radiocarbon or U/Th, and their time axes come from an age model. If we want to incorporate age uncertainty into our analyses, geoChronR can help with this.
geoChronR handles this with age ensembles: many plausible age models (typically 1000), each a potential time axis for the record. Any analysis run on every ensemble member gives a distribution of results instead of a single answer.
In this tutorial we:
The example is Crevice Lake, Yellowstone National Park (LS08STCR; Stevens and Dean, 2008). Its calcite d18O is interpreted as a record of streamflow (larger values, less streamflow), and it is one of the records in the WNA composite in tutorial 2.

title: 3. Age uncertainty with geoChronR
text:
Setup
library(geoChronR) loads the whole family: lipdR, ens, lipdViz and agemodelR.

library(geoChronR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

source(here::here("R/helpers.R"))
checkVersions()

D <- getHydroclimate2k()
L <- D[["LS08STCR"]]
L$geo$siteName

[1] "Crevice"

title: 3. Age uncertainty with geoChronR
text:
What dating information is there?
Dating information lives in chronData, separate from the proxy data in paleoData. Each chronData can hold measurement tables (the dates themselves) and models (age models built from them).

chron <- lipdR::getMeasurementTables(L,pc = "chron") 
  
chron[[1]]


  



There are 12 radiocarbon dates and one calendar age, the 7,627 yr BP tephra at 313 cm (most likely the Mazama ash).






TipExploring a dataset



lipdR::getTables(L,pc = "chron) return the tables as data frames. In an interactive session, selectData(L) with no var.name lists every variable and asks you to pick one.

title: 3. Age uncertainty with geoChronR
section: The age ensemble that came with the dataset
text:
The age ensemble that came with the dataset
This dataset already includes an age model with a 1,000-member ensemble:

existing <- L$chronData[[1]]$model[[1]]$ensembleTable[[1]]
dim(existing$ageEnsemble$values)   # depths x ensemble members

[1]  102 1000

existing$ageEnsemble$units

[1] "yr BP"


plotChronEns() shows the ensemble against depth: the median (black), quantile ribbons (grey), a few individual ensemble members (red), and the probability distributions of the dates (purple).

plotChronEns(L, model.num = 1, truncate.dist = 1e-4) +
  ggtitle("Crevice Lake: age model from the dataset")

title: 3. Age uncertainty with geoChronR
section: Build a new age model with Bchron
text:
Build a new age model with Bchron
You’ll often want to build your own model: to use updated calibration curves, change assumptions, or because the dataset has dates but no model. agemodelR runs Bacon, Bchron, BAM and OxCal on LiPD data. Here we use Bchron, which is quick and runs anywhere.
First, a constraint for the core top. The original age model puts the sediment surface (0 cm) at 1993 CE, which is -43 yr BP. Without a surface age, Bchron extrapolates freely above the shallowest date at 20 cm, and the youngest samples end up with ages in the future. We might want to add that the LiPD file, but for now we add the surface age as a calendar date with a small uncertainty:

chron <- L$chronData[[1]]$measurementTable[[1]]
for (v in names(chron)) {
  if (is.list(chron[[v]]) && !is.null(chron[[v]]$values)) {
    chron[[v]]$values <- c(NA, chron[[v]]$values)
  }
}
chron$depth$values[1] <- 0
chron$age$values[1] <- -43     # 1993 CE
chron$`SD-1`$values[1] <- 5
L$chronData[[1]]$measurementTable[[1]] <- chron

Now run Bchron. Giving all the arguments explicitly lets it run without asking questions. Rows with a radiocarbon age are calibrated with IntCal20, and rows with only a calendar age (our core top and the tephra) are treated as calendar ages. We store the result as model 2, so the original model stays in place.

set.seed(2026)
L <- runBchron(L,
               chron.num = 1,
               meas.table.num = 1,
               model.num = 2,
               cal.curves = "intcal20",
               iter = 10000,
               ask = FALSE,
               lab.id.var = "labID",
               age.14c.var = "age14C",
               age.14c.uncertainty.var = "SD",
               age.var = "age",
               age.uncertainty.var = "SD-1",
               depth.var = "depth",
               reservoir.age.14c.var = NULL,
               reservoir.age.14c.uncertainty.var = NULL,
               rejected.ages.var = NULL)

This takes a few minutes. When you’re experimenting, lower iter (with ask = FALSE) to make it faster.

plotChronEns(L, model.num = 2, truncate.dist = 1e-4) +
  ggtitle("Crevice Lake: new Bchron age model")

title: 3. Age uncertainty with geoChronR
section: Put the ensemble on the proxy data
text:
Put the ensemble on the proxy data
The age model gives ages at a regular set of depths. mapAgeEnsembleToPaleoData() interpolates every ensemble member to the depths of the d18O samples and adds an ageEnsemble column to the paleo measurement table.

L <- mapAgeEnsembleToPaleoData(L,
                               age.var = "ageEnsemble",
                               chron.num = 1, model.num = 2,
                               paleo.num = 1, paleo.meas.table.num = 1)

selectData() pulls a variable out of a table, together with its units and metadata:

ageEns  <- selectData(L, var.name = "ageEnsemble", paleo.or.chron.num = 1, meas.table.num = 1)
d18O    <- selectData(L, var.name = "d18O",        paleo.or.chron.num = 1, meas.table.num = 1)
yearPub <- selectData(L, var.name = "year",        paleo.or.chron.num = 1, meas.table.num = 1)


dim(ageEns$values)   # samples x ensemble members

[1]  277 1000

ageEns$units

[1] "yr BP"


The ensemble is in yr BP. convertBP2AD() converts it to years CE, using year CE = 1950 - yr BP:

yearEns <- convertBP2AD(ageEns)
yearEns$units

[1] "AD"

title: 3. Age uncertainty with geoChronR
section: Plot the record with its age uncertainty
text:
Plot the record with its age uncertainty
plotTimeseriesEnsRibbons() shows the spread of the ensemble as quantile ribbons, and plotTimeseriesEnsLines() adds a few individual members. Here we also add the published time axis (blue) and an axis in yr BP on top.

plotTimeseriesEnsRibbons(X = yearEns, Y = d18O, n.bins = 400) |>
  plotTimeseriesEnsLines(X = yearEns, Y = d18O, n.ens.plot = 5, color = "Reds", alp = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(x = yearPub$values, y = d18O$values), color = "blue", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous("Year (CE)", sec.axis = sec_axis(~ 1950 - ., name = "Age (yr BP)")) +
  labs(y = "d18O (permil)", title = "Crevice Lake d18O with age uncertainty") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








Zoom in on the Common Era:

plotTimeseriesEnsRibbons(X = yearEns, Y = d18O, n.bins = 400) |>
  plotTimeseriesEnsLines(X = yearEns, Y = d18O, n.ens.plot = 5, color = "Reds", alp = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(x = yearPub$values, y = d18O$values), color = "blue", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous("Year (CE)", sec.axis = sec_axis(~ 1950 - ., name = "Age (yr BP)")) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 2000), ylim = c(-10.5, -4.5)) +
  labs(y = "d18O (permil)") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")








How uncertain is the age of each sample? The width of the 95% range of the ensemble:

tibble(year = apply(yearEns$values, 1, median, na.rm = TRUE),
       width = apply(yearEns$values, 1, \(x) diff(quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975), na.rm = TRUE)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, width)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year (CE, ensemble median)", y = "95% age range (years)") +
  theme_bw()








Ages are best constrained near the dates and worst where dates are far apart. The 133 cm gap between the dates at 122 and 255 cm leaves the middle Holocene uncertain by more than 2,000 years. In the Common Era the 95% range is about 200 to 500 years, which is enough to blur the timing of century-scale events. Compare the binned draws below.

title: 3. Age uncertainty with geoChronR
section: Use the ensemble in a composite
text:
Use the ensemble in a composite
compositeR and actR use an age ensemble whenever a record has one. In tutorial 2 every record had a single time axis, so compositeR simulated age uncertainty with BAM. To use the Bchron ensemble instead, put the matrix (in yr BP) in the record’s ageEnsemble column:

h2k <- h2kTimeseries()

crevice <- h2k |> filter(dataSetName == "LS08STCR", paleoData_variableName == "d18O")
nrow(crevice)

[1] 1

length(crevice$time[[1]]) == nrow(ageEns$values)

[1] TRUE

crevice$ageEnsemble <- list(ageEns$values)
crevice$ageEnsembleUnits <- "yr BP"

lipdR::getTsTime() returns a record’s time axis on any scale. When there is an age ensemble it returns that, as a matrix:

dim(lipdR::getTsTime(crevice, units = "CE"))

[1]  277 1000


compositeEnsembles() does this for every record. Its binning function, sampleEnsembleThenBinTs(), picks a random column (one complete age model) each time it bins the record. We can call it directly, and tell it to bin on the ageEnsemble column, converted to years CE:

binvec <- seq(0, 2000, by = 20)

set.seed(1)
draws <- replicate(20, compositeR::sampleEnsembleThenBinTs(crevice, binvec,
                                                           time.variable = "ageEnsemble",
                                                           time.units = "CE",
                                                           defaultUnc = 0))

tibble(year = rep(binvec[-1] - 10, 20), d18O = as.vector(draws), draw = rep(1:20, each = length(binvec) - 1)) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, d18O, group = draw)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Year (CE)", y = "d18O (permil)", title = "20 binned draws from the age ensemble") +
  theme_bw()








To use it in tutorial 2’s composite, add the ageEnsemble column to the Crevice Lake row of h2k before selecting and clipping the records (clipTime() clips the ensemble too), and the composite carries the radiocarbon-based age uncertainty instead of the BAM approximation.

title: 3. Age uncertainty with geoChronR
text:
Try this

Plot the original ensemble (model 1) and the new one (model 2) on the same axes. Where do they differ, and why might they?
Rerun Bchron without the core-top constraint and look at the youngest samples.
Build a Bacon model with runBacon(). It is slower, but it models changes in accumulation rate.
Pick another lake from the WNA table in tutorial 2, check its chronData, and build its age model.
ens has age-uncertain correlation (corEns()) and regression (regressEns()). Try correlating Crevice Lake with a nearby tree-ring streamflow record.
